theme: Nineveh repents; Jonah’s anger, God’s mercy
readingInstruction: Read Jonah 3:1-4:11. God commands Jonah a second time, Nineveh repents, and Jonah is angry. The book ends with a question and no answer. Read it slowly and ask what the question is asking of you.
settingTheScene: Jonah has been rescued and returned to dry land. The word of the LORD comes to him “a second time.” This is the last scene of a book that began with a runaway prophet. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the cruel empire that would soon destroy the northern kingdom. For Jonah to preach to them and see them spared is a scandal, and the book exposes why.
observation: “Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the second time” (3:1).
“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!” (3:4).
“And the people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and put on sackcloth” (3:5).
“Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish” (3:9).
“When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them” (3:10).
“But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry” (4:1).
“For I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster” (4:2).
“And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?” (4:11).
interpretation:
God gives Jonah a second chance. This is a pattern in Scripture: the God who rescues also recommissions. This time Jonah goes, and his sermon is eight words in Hebrew. There is no call to repent in it, only a warning. Yet the whole city believes. From the greatest to the least they fast and wear sackcloth, and even the king takes off his robe and sits in ashes. The most unlikely audience in the Old Testament responds better than Israel ever did to many prophets.

The king’s reasoning is worth noting: “Who knows? God may turn and relent.” He has no guarantee. He repents on the bare chance of mercy. And God does relent. This does not mean God changed his mind in a way that surprised him. It shows that his threats of judgment are real invitations to repent, and that when people turn, he is always ready to forgive.

Chapter 4 is the real point of the book. Jonah is furious. His prayer reveals why he ran in the first place: “I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.” He quotes the great self-description of God from Exodus 34:6, and he resents it. He did not want Nineveh to be shown the mercy that he himself had just received. The prophet who was rescued from the deep is angry that God rescues others.

God does not rebuke him harshly. He asks a question: “Do you do well to be angry?” Then he uses a plant, a worm, and a scorching wind to teach him. Jonah pities the plant that gave him shade, though he did not make it. Should God not pity a city of 120,000 people, and even the animals?

The book ends with that question, unanswered. We do not know what Jonah did. The question is left for the reader. Will you rejoice in God’s mercy to those you think do not deserve it?
connection: Jesus said that the men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment and condemn the generation that rejected him, “for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41). Jesus told the parable of the prodigal son, which also ends with an angry older brother outside the feast (Luke 15:28-32). 1 Timothy 2:3-4 says God desires all people to be saved. Acts 10:34-35 shows Peter learning that God shows no partiality. 2 Peter 3:9 says God is patient, not wishing that any should perish.
application:
Ask yourself who your “Nineveh” is, a person or group you would rather not see forgiven.

Pray for God to show mercy to someone you find hard to love.

Thank God for giving you a second chance, as he gave Jonah.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the second chance he gave you.
Ask him to search your heart for anger where he is merciful.
Ask him to teach you to care for those you would rather not.
